newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Gingrich hails Taiwan democracy as model for China.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich hails Taiwan democracy as model for China.

text.p: U.S. congressional chief Newt Gingrich ended a whirlwind Asian tour in Taiwan on Wednesday, hailing the Nationalist-ruled island's democracy and capitalist economy as models for communist rival China.

Gingrich, the first U.S. House of Representatives speaker to visit since Washington switched diplomatic ties to Beijing in 1979, stood by his controversial pledge that U.S. forces would defend Taiwan against Chinese attack.
But he urged Taiwan and China to settle their festering differences through peaceful dialogue, not force.
"Taiwan has completed a remarkable journey to full democracy," Gingrich said at the close of a three-hour visit that included a meeting with Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui.

"Taiwan's elected legislature and the recent inauguration of the first popularly elected president in over 4,000 years of Chinese history, provide a model not only for the People's Republic of China, but for the world," the speaker said.
Gingrich, who in his weekend trip to China slammed Beijing for human rights failings, said he told both Lee and China's leaders that force was no key to Taiwan's reunification.
"The use of force or engaging in provocative actions by either side is unacceptable," Gingrich said.

"It's important to be explicit with both the People's Republic of China and Taiwan that should Beijing seek to reunify Taiwan with the mainland by force or intimidation, the United States will use all means necessary to prevent it," he said.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war ended in 1949. Beijing regards the island as a renegade province to be brought under mainland's eventual control, by force if necessary.

Lee seized on the rare visit by a prominent U.S. political figure to restate Taiwan's tough terms, telling Gingrich that Taipei would never accept "communist China's attempt to regard Taiwan as one of its provinces."
"We maintain that 'one China' will be achieved when the two sides of the strait reunite under democracy and freedom," Lee was quoted by his office as saying in their hourlong meeting.
It was Lee's private but high-profile 1995 visit to New York that prompted a furious Beijing to suspend cross-strait talks and launch eight months of threatening war games near Taiwan.

The sabre-rattling, which preceded Taiwan's historic March 1996 direct presidential election, led Washington to deploy two aircraft carriers to the region -- its largest Asian armada since the Vietnam War.
Beijing alleged that Lee's trip and the election were plots by the island to assert independence from mainland sovereignty.
Taiwan says it wants to reunify with China if Beijing launches democratic reforms, but the island maintains the right to conduct its own affairs under current separation.
Gingrich called on Taipei and Beijing to start talking, saying dialogue was "the best available mechanism for achieving a long-term, peaceful resolution of the differences".

Despite Washington's show of support for Taiwan during Beijing's war games, U.S. officials had sought to play down Gingrich's assurances of U.S. military protection, saying his view did not represent those of the Clinton administration.
China warned the U.S. on Tuesday not to interfere in Beijing's dealings with Taiwan, saying Washington should halt its large-scale high-technology weapons sales to Taipei.
It opposes U.S. arms sales and any American attempts to protect Taiwan as interference in China's internal affairs.
U.S. law authorises Washington to offer defensive arms to Taiwan but is ambiguous on whether the United States would come to the Nationalist-ruled island's defence.
